title: Type Coercion and Equality
description: How == quietly converts operand types, why === usually wins, and the handful of exceptions worth memorizing.

blocks.content: `===` compares value and type with no conversion. `==` first coerces operands toward a common type using a fixed set of rules (e.g. comparing against `null`/`undefined` only matches each other; numbers vs strings convert the string to a number) before comparing. `Object.is()` behaves like `===` except it treats `NaN` as equal to itself and distinguishes `+0` from `-0`.
keyPoints: `null == undefined` is `true`, but `null === undefined` is `false` — this is one of the few places `==` is arguably useful (checking for 'either null or undefined').
Object equality (`===` or `==`) always compares references, never structural/deep content, for both operators.
`NaN === NaN` is `false` — use `Number.isNaN()` or `Object.is(x, NaN)` to actually detect NaN.

blocks.code:
'5' + 1;      // '51'  (+ concatenates when either side is a string)
'5' - 1;      // 4     (- always coerces to numbers)
0 == false;   // true  (loose equality coerces)
0 === false;  // false (strict equality does not)
Object.is(NaN, NaN); // true
blocks.explanation: `+` is the one arithmetic operator that also means string concatenation, which is why it coerces differently from `-`, `*`, `/`.

blocks.question: What does `[] == false` evaluate to, and why?
blocks.answer: true.
blocks.explanation: `==` coercion rules convert both sides toward numbers when one side is a boolean: `false` becomes `0`, and the empty array `[]` is first converted to a primitive via `toString()` (yielding `""`), then `""` converts to `0` — so the comparison becomes `0 == 0`, which is true. This is exactly the kind of surprising chain that makes `===` the recommended default: it never engages this conversion machinery at all.

title: ES6 Classes and Private Fields
description: Class syntax as sugar over prototypes, and real, language-enforced privacy with #private fields.

blocks.content: `class` syntax builds on the same prototype-based inheritance JavaScript already had — methods declared in a class body are installed on `ClassName.prototype` and shared by every instance, exactly like the manual `Constructor.prototype.method = ...` pattern. `#privateField` syntax adds true, engine-enforced privacy: unlike a `_conventionallyPrivate` property, code outside the class cannot read, write, or even detect a `#field`'s existence.
keyPoints: Class methods are non-enumerable on the prototype, unlike properties assigned in the constructor.
`#private` fields are scoped to the class body lexically — even a subclass cannot access a parent's `#field` directly.
`static` members belong to the class itself, not instances, and are commonly used for factory methods or shared constants.

blocks.explanation: `#balance` cannot be read, mutated, or even referenced from outside `BankAccount` — this is real privacy enforced by the JavaScript engine, not just a naming convention like `_balance`.

blocks.question: What happens when this runs?
blocks.answer: 1, then undefined (accessing `c['#count']` does not reach the private field).
blocks.explanation: `#count` is not a regular string-keyed property — bracket notation with the literal string `'#count'` looks up an ordinary (non-existent) property named `#count`, not the private field, which can only be accessed via `this.#count` from inside the class body.

title: ES Modules and Dynamic Import
description: Static import/export boundaries, and using dynamic import() for runtime code-splitting.

blocks.content: ES modules use static `import`/`export` declarations, resolved and validated before any module code runs — this static structure is what lets bundlers tree-shake unused exports. `import()` (as a function call, not a declaration) is dynamic: it returns a Promise that resolves to the module's namespace object, and it's the standard mechanism behind route-level and on-demand code splitting.
keyPoints: Static imports are hoisted and resolved at parse time; dynamic `import()` can appear anywhere, including inside conditionals and event handlers.
A dynamically-imported chunk is only downloaded when the `import()` call actually executes — this is exactly how Angular's `loadComponent`/`loadChildren` route lazy-loading works under the hood.
Circular ES module dependencies are allowed but can leave one side seeing a partially-initialized export if not handled carefully.

blocks.explanation: The heavy charting library's bytes never reach the browser until `openAnalytics()` is actually called, keeping the initial bundle small.

blocks.question: Why can bundlers tree-shake unused exports from static ES modules but generally cannot from CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`)?
blocks.answer: Static `import`/`export` declarations form a graph that's fully knowable without executing any code — a bundler can see exactly which named exports are imported and drop the rest. CommonJS's `require()` and `module.exports` are just regular function calls and object mutations that happen at runtime, so a bundler generally can't prove which properties of an exported object are actually used without executing the module.
blocks.explanation: This static analyzability is one of the concrete practical reasons the ecosystem moved from CommonJS to ES modules, beyond just syntax preference.

title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
description: How the engine decides what to reclaim, and the common patterns that accidentally keep things alive.

blocks.content: JavaScript engines garbage-collect by tracing reachability from a set of roots (global object, active call stacks, closures still in scope) — anything unreachable from a root is eventually reclaimed. "Memory leaks" in JS almost always mean something is unintentionally still reachable, not that the engine failed to collect it. `WeakMap`/`WeakSet` hold their keys weakly, so entries don't by themselves keep an object alive.
keyPoints: Common leak sources: event listeners never removed, `setInterval` timers never cleared, module-level caches that grow unbounded, and closures capturing more than they need.
GC timing is nondeterministic and not something application code controls or should rely on for cleanup ordering.
Use `WeakMap` to attach metadata to an object (e.g. a DOM node) without preventing that object from being garbage-collected once nothing else references it.

blocks.explanation: The first version has no way to ever detach the listener, so `controller` — and its whole closure chain — stays reachable from `window` for the page's entire lifetime. The second version returns a cleanup function that removes the listener when the consumer is done.

blocks.question: A single-page app's memory usage climbs steadily every time the user navigates between two routes, never coming back down. How would you find and fix the leak?
blocks.answer: Take heap snapshots (DevTools Memory tab) before and after several navigation cycles and diff retained object counts to find what's growing. Look specifically at event listeners attached to long-lived targets (`window`, `document`) that aren't removed on route/component teardown, timers (`setInterval`/`setTimeout`) never cleared, and subscriptions (RxJS, WebSocket) never unsubscribed. Fix by cleaning up in the component/route's teardown hook (e.g. Angular's `ngOnDestroy`), matching every `addEventListener`/`subscribe`/`setInterval` with a corresponding removal.
blocks.explanation: This is the standard framework-agnostic memory-leak triage process, and it's exactly why lifecycle cleanup hooks exist in every major frontend framework.

title: Event loop under production load
description: Senior/lead scenario: A click handler starts CPU-heavy work, several promises, and a setTimeout. The UI freezes and logs appear in an unexpected order. Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Think of the main thread as a single checkout lane. A promise changes when code runs, but it does not give JavaScript another lane for CPU work.

Microtasks are high priority cleanup work after the current stack, so they run before timers and before the browser moves on. That is useful for promise consistency, but dangerous if the microtask queue never empties.

The production question is how to keep the UI responsive while the work still finishes correctly.
keyPoints: JavaScript executes one task at a time on the main thread. Promise callbacks are queued as microtasks and are normally drained before the next task such as setTimeout or user input.
A long synchronous function blocks rendering, input, timers, and promise continuation. Splitting work only with more promises can still starve rendering because microtasks can run continuously.
Reduce the work, process in chunks that yield to the browser, move CPU-heavy computation to a Web Worker, or move aggregation to the backend.
Use the Performance panel to identify long tasks and verify improvement on representative devices.
Explain ordering using call stack, task queue, microtask queue, and rendering opportunity rather than memorized output only.

blocks.question: A click handler starts CPU-heavy work, several promises, and a setTimeout. The UI freezes and logs appear in an unexpected order. Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.
blocks.answer:
JavaScript runs one piece of work at a time on the main thread. If the click handler starts a long CPU-heavy function, that function owns the thread until it returns. During that time the browser cannot paint, handle input, run timers, or continue promise callbacks.

The log order comes from the queues. Synchronous code runs first. Promise callbacks go into the microtask queue. setTimeout goes into the task queue, and it normally waits until the current task and the pending microtasks are done.

A common trap is trying to fix heavy work by wrapping it in promises. That does not make CPU work parallel. If microtasks keep scheduling more microtasks, the browser can still be starved and never get a good chance to render.

In production I would reduce the work, chunk it with real yields back to the browser, or move the CPU-heavy part to a Web Worker. If the work is really aggregation or reporting, I would also ask whether it belongs on the backend.

I would verify the fix in the Performance panel, looking for long tasks, input delay, and frame drops on realistic devices. The right answer is not just the memorized log order; it is explaining the call stack, task queue, microtask queue, and the browser's chance to paint.

blocks.answer: If a promise callback recursively schedules another promise callback forever, the microtask queue never drains. Timers, rendering, and user input can be starved because the browser keeps running microtasks before moving to the next task. In practice the page may look frozen even though JavaScript is still busy.

title: Closures in a long-lived application
description: Senior/lead scenario: A function returns callbacks that reference a large dataset. Even after the screen is closed, memory remains high. How can closures cause this?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Closures are about reachability. The garbage collector does not care that a screen is visually gone; it cares whether something can still be reached from roots like window, timers, DOM listeners, or module-level caches.

The mental model is: callback retained means captured scope retained. Good design keeps callback lifetimes clear and captures the smallest stable values needed.
keyPoints: A closure retains access to variables from its lexical environment as long as the callback remains reachable.
If a listener, timer, cache, or global registry keeps the callback, the captured dataset and related objects can remain alive even when the UI is gone.
Remove listeners and timers, release registry entries, capture only required values, and avoid closing over entire component or response objects.
Use heap snapshots and retaining paths to prove what holds the callback.
Closures are not inherently leaks; incorrect lifetime and reachability are the problem.

blocks.question: A function returns callbacks that reference a large dataset. Even after the screen is closed, memory remains high. How can closures cause this?
blocks.answer:
A closure keeps access to variables from the scope where it was created. That is normal JavaScript behavior and often very useful. The problem starts when the callback lives longer than the screen or object that created it.

If a timer, event listener, cache, or global registry still points to the callback, the callback is reachable. Anything it captured can stay reachable too, including a large dataset, a response object, or a whole component instance.

I would fix the lifetime first. Remove listeners, clear timers, unregister from caches, and clean up subscriptions when the screen closes. I would also avoid capturing more than the callback needs.

For example, instead of closing over a huge record list, capture a small ID and read current data from a store when the callback runs. That keeps the callback useful without making it own the old data by accident.

To prove the issue, I would use heap snapshots and retaining paths. Closures are not leaks by themselves; leaks happen when reachable callbacks hold data past the intended lifetime.

title: Understanding this in callbacks
description: Senior/lead scenario: A class method works when called directly but fails when passed as an event callback because this becomes undefined. Explain and solve it.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Think of this as a call-site rule, not a declaration rule. The same function can receive different this values depending on whether it is called as obj.fn(), fn(), fn.call(x), or by an event system.

Arrows are different because they do not have their own this, arguments, or prototype. They are useful for callbacks, but they are not constructors and are not always the best fit for prototype-based behavior.
keyPoints: For regular functions, this is determined by the call site, not where the function was declared. Passing obj.method loses the obj receiver.
Use an arrow wrapper, bind once, or define a class-field arrow function when stable lexical this is desired.
Do not call bind repeatedly during rendering because every call creates a new function and complicates removal of listeners.
Arrow functions do not have their own this, arguments, or prototype and should not be used as constructors.
Choose an approach based on identity, memory, inheritance, and testability.

blocks.question: A class method works when called directly but fails when passed as an event callback because this becomes undefined. Explain and solve it.
blocks.answer:
For a normal function, this is decided by how the function is called. It is not locked to the place where the method was written. So obj.method() has obj as the receiver, but passing obj.method as a callback passes only the function.

When the event system calls that function later, the original object is gone from the call site. In strict mode, this may be undefined. In browser event handlers, this may also be set by the event system instead of your class instance.

I would fix it by making the receiver stable. Good options are an arrow wrapper, binding once in the constructor, or using a class-field arrow method when lexical this is the intended behavior.

I would not call bind every time the component renders or every time I add and remove a listener. Each bind call creates a new function, which makes identity-based cleanup harder and can add unnecessary allocations.

The choice depends on identity, memory, inheritance, and tests. Arrow methods are simple, bound methods are explicit, and prototype methods still work well when the call site keeps the receiver.

blocks.answer: removeEventListener needs the exact same function object that was passed to addEventListener. obj.method.bind(obj) creates a new function each time it is called. If add uses one bound function and remove creates another, the browser cannot match them, so the listener stays installed.

title: Prototype chain and inheritance
description: Senior/lead scenario: A library extends built-in objects and patches prototypes globally. What risks does this create?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The prototype chain is shared behavior. That is powerful for language features, but global mutation turns a local helper into application-wide behavior.

A senior way to think about it is blast radius. If a change affects every array, object, or string in the runtime, it needs a very strong reason and careful isolation.
keyPoints: Property lookup walks the prototype chain, so global prototype changes affect every instance and may collide with future platform or library properties.
Enumerable prototype additions can break code that iterates with for...in without ownership checks.
Monkey patching makes behavior order-dependent and difficult to isolate in tests or multiple application versions.
Prefer composition, utility functions, subclasses under controlled boundaries, or symbols for non-colliding metadata.
Use Object.hasOwn when ownership matters and avoid assuming prototype properties are data fields.

blocks.question: A library extends built-in objects and patches prototypes globally. What risks does this create?
blocks.answer:
JavaScript property lookup walks the object first and then its prototype chain. If a library changes a built-in prototype, it changes lookup behavior for every matching value in the application. That can collide with future platform APIs or with another library.

Enumerable prototype additions are especially risky. Code using for...in can start seeing inherited names that were never meant to be data fields. If that code does not check ownership, business logic can break in strange ways.

Monkey patching also makes behavior depend on load order. Tests may pass when one patch is installed first and fail when another bundle or version changes the order.

I would prefer composition, utility functions, or controlled subclasses when we own the boundary. If metadata needs to live beside an object, a Symbol or WeakMap is often safer than adding global prototype properties.

When ownership matters, I would use Object.hasOwn or another own-property check. I would not assume everything found by property lookup is actual data on the object.

title: Equality and coercion in business rules
description: Senior/lead scenario: An API sometimes returns "0", 0, null, and an empty string. A developer uses loose equality to simplify checks. What problems can occur?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Coercion is a convenience feature, not a good business boundary. The problem is not that loose equality always fails; it is that readers must remember a large set of conversion rules while also reading domain logic.

Good systems turn messy outside data into clean inside data once. Then the rest of the code can be strict, boring, and easier to test.
keyPoints: Loose equality performs coercion with rules that are difficult to reason about in mixed input data. Values such as 0, false, and empty string may compare in surprising ways.
Normalize external input at the boundary into an explicit domain type, then use strict equality inside the application.
Distinguish missing, empty, zero, and false because they often represent different business states.
Use nullish coalescing when only null or undefined should trigger a default; logical OR also treats other falsy values as absent.
Add contract validation and tests for all boundary variants rather than relying on coercion.

blocks.question: An API sometimes returns "0", 0, null, and an empty string. A developer uses loose equality to simplify checks. What problems can occur?
blocks.answer:
Loose equality can hide important differences in mixed API data. Values like 0, false, an empty string, and null often mean different things to the business. Coercion can make those differences disappear at the worst place.

I would normalize external input at the boundary. After parsing the API response, the app should have clear domain values: missing, empty, zero, and false should be represented on purpose.

Inside the application, I would use strict equality against those normalized values. That makes rules easier to read and avoids surprising comparisons when new API variants appear.

Defaults need the same care. value || default treats 0, false, and an empty string as absent. value ?? default only falls back for null or undefined.

I would add contract validation and tests for every boundary case the API can send. Relying on coercion is not a data model; it is a hidden rule nobody owns.

title: Deep cloning application state
description: Senior/lead scenario: A team uses JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) to deep-clone state before editing. What is wrong with this approach?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Cloning is not just copying bytes. It is deciding what identity, type, prototype, and ownership mean after the copy.

The simple mental split is JSON data, structured clone data, and domain objects with behavior. Each group needs a different approach, and large state often needs targeted immutable updates instead of whole-tree cloning.
keyPoints: JSON serialization loses undefined, functions, symbols, BigInt, Map, Set, typed arrays, prototypes, and special object semantics; dates become strings and cycles fail.
It can be expensive for large objects and hides an architecture problem when only a small immutable update was required.
Use structuredClone for supported structured data, a domain-specific copy function, or immutable updates that copy only changed paths.
Do not clone class instances blindly; define how identity and behavior should be preserved.
Measure memory and CPU when cloning large state and prefer normalized data.

blocks.question: A team uses JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) to deep-clone state before editing. What is wrong with this approach?
blocks.answer:
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) is not a safe general deep clone. It only preserves JSON data. It drops undefined, functions, symbols, and special object behavior, and it cannot handle cycles.

It also changes data. Dates become strings. Map, Set, typed arrays, BigInt, class instances, and prototypes either fail or lose meaning. That can quietly corrupt application state.

Performance is another issue. Cloning a large state tree just to edit one field creates extra CPU work and memory pressure. Often it points to a design problem: only the changed path needed a new copy.

For structured data, structuredClone may be a better built-in choice, but it is still not a design answer for every case. For domain objects, I would write a copy function that states what identity and behavior should be preserved.

In UI state, I usually prefer normalized data and immutable updates that copy only changed branches. Then I would measure memory and CPU on realistic state sizes.

title: Protecting Aadhaar while allowing other bank-account updates
description: Senior/lead scenario: A bank-account object contains accountHolderName, mobileNumber, address, nominee and aadhaarNumber. The business rule says Aadhaar cannot be changed after KYC verification, but the other properties can be updated. How would you enforce this in JavaScript, and what limitations would you explain?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
This is an immutability rule for one sensitive field, not a reason to freeze the whole model. Protect the invariant at every boundary where data can be changed or recreated.

Object descriptors are local JavaScript tools. Security and compliance rules must live on the trusted server side too, because client code can always be bypassed.
keyPoints: Use Object.defineProperty with writable: false and configurable: false to protect only the Aadhaar property on one object instance.
Do not use Object.freeze when other account properties must remain editable.
Whitelist editable fields when creating update payloads; object spread can otherwise create a new object with a changed Aadhaar value.
The backend must enforce immutable KYC identity fields and record tampering attempts in audit logs.

blocks.question: A bank-account object contains accountHolderName, mobileNumber, address, nominee and aadhaarNumber. The business rule says Aadhaar cannot be changed after KYC verification, but the other properties can be updated. How would you enforce this in JavaScript, and what limitations would you explain?
blocks.answer:
I would separate the business rule from the browser first. JavaScript can help prevent accidental changes, but it cannot be the final security boundary. The backend must reject attempts to change a verified Aadhaar number and record tampering attempts.

For a local object, Object.defineProperty can protect only aadhaarNumber. I would set writable: false and configurable: false for that property while leaving accountHolderName, mobileNumber, address, and nominee writable.

I would not use Object.freeze on the whole account. Freeze would make every own data property non-writable, which blocks the updates the business still allows.

The update path matters more than the object descriptor. I would build update payloads from an explicit allowlist of editable fields. Blind object spread or Object.assign can create a new object with a changed Aadhaar value, because descriptors only protect that one object instance.

In production I would combine a read-only UI after KYC, a domain update function that rejects immutable fields, backend enforcement, authorization, and audit logs. I would test direct assignment, spread, Object.assign, JSON round-trips, and tampered network requests.

title: Debounce versus throttle
description: Senior/lead scenario: A search box and a scroll listener both generate too many operations. Would you use debounce or throttle?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Debounce answers: wait until things get quiet. Throttle answers: run at most once per time window.

The right choice depends on whether intermediate states matter. Search usually cares about the final text; scrolling often cares about progress during the movement.
keyPoints: Debounce waits for a quiet period and is suitable for search input where intermediate values are usually not useful.
Throttle limits execution frequency and is suitable for continuous events such as scroll or pointer movement where periodic updates are useful.

blocks.question: A search box and a scroll listener both generate too many operations. Would you use debounce or throttle?
blocks.answer:
For the search box, I would usually debounce. The user may type five characters quickly, and the intermediate queries are often not useful. Waiting for a short quiet period reduces request volume and avoids wasted UI work.

For scroll or pointer movement, I would usually throttle. The event is continuous, and the UI often needs periodic updates while the user is still moving. Throttle gives a steady maximum rate instead of waiting until everything stops.

The details matter. I would decide whether the first call should run immediately, whether the last call should be guaranteed, and what happens when the component unmounts.

Debounce alone does not solve search races. I would normalize the query, skip duplicate values, cancel stale requests when possible, and ignore older responses if they still arrive.

For some scroll or resize work, I would avoid manual listeners entirely. IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, CSS, or virtualization can remove the high-frequency work from my code.

title: Promise error propagation
description: Senior/lead scenario: A promise chain logs an error but later code continues with undefined data. Explain how errors propagate and how to design the chain.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A promise chain is a value pipeline with two tracks: fulfilled and rejected. catch can move the pipeline from rejected back to fulfilled if it returns a normal value.

That makes recovery explicit, but it also means logging is not neutral. After logging, the code must choose whether to recover with a real fallback or keep the failure visible.
keyPoints: Throwing inside then rejects the returned promise. A catch handles the rejection and, if it returns a normal value, converts the chain back to fulfilled.
Catch at a level that can actually recover. Re-throw or return a rejected promise when the caller must know the operation failed.
Use finally only for cleanup; its callback does not receive the result and should not replace it accidentally.
Avoid mixing callbacks, unreturned promises, and async functions because errors can escape the intended chain.
Install global unhandled-rejection telemetry as a last-resort signal, not as business error handling.

blocks.question: A promise chain logs an error but later code continues with undefined data. Explain how errors propagate and how to design the chain.
blocks.answer:
In a promise chain, throwing inside a then callback rejects the promise returned by that then. A catch handles a rejection. If the catch returns a normal value, the chain becomes fulfilled again with that value.

That is why later code can continue with undefined data. The catch logged the error and then implicitly returned undefined, so the next then received undefined as a successful result.

I would catch errors at a level that can actually recover. If the operation failed and the caller must know, the catch should rethrow or return a rejected promise after logging or cleanup.

finally is for cleanup, not for producing the business result. Its callback does not receive the fulfilled value in the same way then does, and it should not accidentally hide the real outcome.

I would also avoid mixing callbacks, unreturned promises, and async functions in the same flow. Unreturned work can fail outside the intended chain, so global unhandled-rejection telemetry should be a last-resort signal, not the main error handling design.

title: Async/await with parallel work
description: Senior/lead scenario: A page waits for five independent APIs sequentially because each call is awaited one by one. How would you optimize it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
await is a pause point in the current async function. It does not automatically know which operations are independent.

The useful mental model is a dependency graph. Start nodes that have no dependency, wait where edges require it, and cap concurrency when the graph is large.
keyPoints: Start independent operations before awaiting, then use Promise.all when all must succeed or Promise.allSettled when partial results are acceptable.
Keep truly dependent operations sequential. Parallelism should reflect dependencies, not a blanket rule.
Bound concurrency when processing many requests to avoid overloading browser connections or the backend.
Propagate cancellation and define timeout/error behavior for each request.
Measure whether the critical path improves and whether one slow optional dependency should be deferred.

blocks.question: A page waits for five independent APIs sequentially because each call is awaited one by one. How would you optimize it?
blocks.answer:
async and await make asynchronous code easier to read, but await still waits. If five independent API calls are awaited one by one, the page creates an artificial waterfall.

I would start the independent operations first and then await them together. Promise.all is right when all five are required for the page to succeed. Promise.allSettled is better when the page can show partial results.

I would keep real dependencies sequential. If call B needs an ID from call A, that part should wait. Parallelism should match the dependency graph, not a blanket rule.

For many requests, I would bound concurrency. Starting hundreds of fetches at once can overload browser connection limits, the backend, or the user's network.

Production code also needs cancellation, timeouts, and clear error behavior. I would measure the critical path and decide whether slow optional data can be deferred until after the main page is usable.

title: Cancelling fetch requests
description: Senior/lead scenario: A component starts a fetch request and is removed before the response arrives. How do you cancel it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Cancellation is part of the operation's contract. The caller needs a way to say this result no longer matters, and lower layers need to honor that signal.

AbortController is the browser's standard shape for this, but safe UI code also needs relevance checks for late or non-cancellable results.
keyPoints: Create an AbortController, pass its signal to fetch, and call abort when the request becomes irrelevant.
Treat AbortError as cancellation rather than a user-facing failure.
Propagate signals through helper layers so lower-level utilities do not hide cancellation.
Cancellation prevents continued work where supported, but code must still guard against late results from non-cancellable sources.
Use one controller per logical operation or compose signals carefully; reusing an already-aborted signal causes immediate rejection.

blocks.question: A component starts a fetch request and is removed before the response arrives. How do you cancel it?
blocks.answer:
For fetch, I would create an AbortController for the logical operation. I would pass controller.signal into fetch and call controller.abort() when the component unmounts, the query changes, or the user cancels.

AbortError should be treated as cancellation, not as a user-facing failure. It usually means the result is no longer relevant.

The signal needs to flow through helper layers. If a data client hides fetch and does not accept a signal, the component cannot cancel the real work.

Cancellation is not the whole story. Some work may not be cancellable, or it may finish right as cleanup happens, so the code should still guard against applying late results to dead UI.

I would use one controller per logical operation, or compose signals carefully. Reusing a signal that has already been aborted causes immediate rejection, which can create confusing bugs.

title: Preventing stale async updates
description: Senior/lead scenario: Two asynchronous operations update the same UI state and can complete out of order. The API cannot be cancelled. What can you do?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
Async code needs a relevance check. Starting work creates a version of intent, and finishing work must check whether that intent is still the current one.

Client-side request IDs are good for UI freshness. Server-side versions are needed when the operation changes durable data.
keyPoints: Assign a monotonically increasing request ID or capture the current query version when starting the operation.
Before applying the result, verify that its ID still matches the latest active operation.
For mutations, use server-side versioning and idempotency; client-side latest-wins is not sufficient for data integrity.
Model operation state explicitly: idle, pending, succeeded, failed, and superseded.

blocks.question: Two asynchronous operations update the same UI state and can complete out of order. The API cannot be cancelled. What can you do?
blocks.answer:
If two async operations can finish out of order, the latest result is not always the last one to arrive. When the API cannot be cancelled, I would make each operation prove it is still current before it updates state.

A common approach is a monotonically increasing request ID. When starting a request, capture the current ID. When it resolves, compare that captured ID with the latest active ID.

If the IDs do not match, the result is stale and should be ignored or marked superseded. The UI state should model that clearly: idle, pending, succeeded, failed, and superseded are different states.

For reads, latest-wins is often fine. For mutations, it is not enough. Data integrity needs server-side versioning, idempotency keys, or conflict handling.

I would test this with controlled promises that resolve in the wrong order. Waiting for the network to randomly reproduce a race is not a real test.

title: Retry with exponential backoff
description: Senior/lead scenario: A frontend retries every failed API immediately and creates a traffic spike during an outage. Design a safer retry strategy.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
A retry is a distributed-systems decision, not just a loop. The client must ask: is this safe to repeat, is the service asking us to slow down, and will many clients do the same thing at once?

Backoff, jitter, caps, and idempotency keep retries from causing more harm than the original failure.
keyPoints: Retry only transient failures and only operations that are idempotent or protected by an idempotency key.
Use exponential backoff with jitter so clients do not retry in lockstep.
Respect Retry-After, cap attempts and total time, and stop on user cancellation or authentication failure.
Surface degraded state and allow manual retry when automatic attempts are exhausted.
Coordinate with backend rate limits and circuit-breaker behavior; the frontend should not amplify an incident.

blocks.question: A frontend retries every failed API immediately and creates a traffic spike during an outage. Design a safer retry strategy.
blocks.answer:
Immediate retries can turn one outage into a bigger outage. If every client retries at once, the frontend becomes a traffic amplifier.

I would retry only failures that look transient, and only for operations that are idempotent or protected by an idempotency key. Retrying a payment or form submit without that protection can duplicate side effects.

The retry delay should use exponential backoff with jitter. Backoff reduces pressure over time, and jitter prevents clients from retrying in the same rhythm.

The strategy should respect Retry-After, cap both attempts and total elapsed time, and stop on user cancellation, logout, or authentication failure.

When automatic retries are exhausted, the UI should show a degraded state and offer manual retry where useful. I would coordinate this with backend rate limits and circuit breakers so the browser does not fight incident recovery.

title: Event delegation for large lists

Delegation uses the DOM's event propagation instead of attaching behavior to every child. One ancestor listener can serve many dynamic rows.

The key is keeping the target matching safe and small: find the action, verify containment, use an ID, and let state remain in JavaScript rather than in the DOM.

Attaching three listeners to each of 20,000 rows creates a lot of functions and lifecycle work. I would move the listener to a stable ancestor and use event bubbling to determine which row and action were targeted.

In the handler, I would use closest with a controlled selector, such as a button with a data-action. I would also verify the matched element belongs to the current table, so clicks from nested or unrelated DOM do not leak in.

I would store stable IDs in data attributes, not large serialized objects. The handler can use the ID to look up the current row data from the application state.

Delegation does not remove accessibility requirements. Keyboard handling, focus, button semantics, and ARIA behavior still need to be correct.

For 20,000 rows, I would also question the DOM size. Event delegation reduces listeners, but virtualization may be needed so the browser is not rendering thousands of off-screen rows.

title: DOM batching and layout thrashing
description: Senior/lead scenario: A loop reads element dimensions and immediately writes styles for hundreds of elements, causing jank. Why?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
The browser wants to batch style, layout, paint, and composite work. JavaScript can accidentally break that batching by asking layout questions after every write.

The simple pattern is read, compute, write. Keep those phases separate and let the browser do fewer larger layout passes.
keyPoints: Alternating layout reads and writes can force the browser to recalculate style and layout repeatedly.
Batch reads first, compute in JavaScript, then batch writes. Use classes or CSS variables rather than many individual style mutations.

blocks.question: A loop reads element dimensions and immediately writes styles for hundreds of elements, causing jank. Why?

The jank comes from mixing layout reads and writes in a loop. When code reads dimensions after changing styles, the browser may be forced to flush style and layout to answer accurately.

If that happens hundreds of times, one logical update turns into repeated recalculation. That is layout thrashing.

I would batch all reads first, compute the needed values in JavaScript, and then batch writes. Using classes or CSS variables is often cleaner than setting many individual style properties.

For visual updates, requestAnimationFrame can align work with the next frame. It is not magic, though; each frame still needs a small amount of work.

I would prefer CSS layout, transforms, and observers like ResizeObserver when they fit. Then I would confirm the fix in the Performance panel by looking for forced reflow, layout cost, and dropped frames.

description: Senior/lead scenario: A JavaScript algorithm takes 800 ms and blocks input. How do you decide whether to use a worker?

A worker gives CPU work another thread, but it also creates a boundary. Everything crossing that boundary must be serialized, cloned, or transferred.

The right mental model is service design inside the browser: define the protocol, errors, cancellation, ownership of data, and how the UI handles late or failed replies.

blocks.question: A JavaScript algorithm takes 800 ms and blocks input. How do you decide whether to use a worker?
blocks.answer:
I would first measure the 800 ms algorithm and confirm it is CPU-heavy. If it blocks input on the main thread and does not need direct DOM access, a Web Worker is a strong option.

A worker is not free. Starting it, sending data, and receiving results all have cost. The job should be large enough or repeated enough to justify that cost.

I would define a small message protocol: request IDs, payload version, success, error, progress, and cancellation or supersession. Without IDs, multiple in-flight jobs become hard to match to results.

For large ArrayBuffers, I would consider transferables so ownership moves instead of copying. For normal objects, structured cloning is convenient but can become expensive with large graphs.

I would avoid shared mutable state unless there is a strong reason for SharedArrayBuffer and the required security headers. Finally, I would plan fallback or graceful degradation if the target environment does not support the worker design.

Lifecycle symmetry matters: every setup path needs a matching teardown path, and cleanup must use the same listener identity.

description: Senior/lead scenario: Implement an in-memory LRU cache for recent API query results. What data structure and policies would you use?

blocks.question: Implement an in-memory LRU cache for recent API query results. What data structure and policies would you use?
blocks.answer:
In JavaScript, a Map is a practical way to build a small LRU cache because it preserves insertion order. On get, if the key exists, I would read the value, delete the key, and set it again so it moves to the most recently used end.

On set, I would also delete an existing key before setting it. If the cache grows beyond capacity, I would evict the oldest key, which is the first key from map.keys().

For a strict textbook O(1) design in lower-level environments, I would use a hash map plus a doubly linked list. In modern JavaScript, Map is often enough unless profiling says otherwise.

Real cache policy matters more than the interview skeleton. I would define capacity, TTL, byte estimate if values are large, tenant or user scoping, explicit invalidation, and what happens when the source API fails.

If caching promises, I would let concurrent callers share the same in-flight work, but remove failed entries so one failure is not cached forever. I would expose hit rate, evictions, and memory metrics.

Formatting is separate from arithmetic. Intl.NumberFormat is good for display, but it should not be the authority for financial totals.

The backend should remain authoritative for transactions. The frontend can preview using the same documented rules, and tests should cover rounding boundaries and cross-currency cases.

I would first identify what kind of date the business means. An instant, a local date-time, and a date-only value are different things. Treating all of them as Date objects creates bugs.

A transaction time is often an instant. I would store it with UTC or an explicit offset and render it in the chosen user, account, or market timezone.

A scheduled local time is different. The rule must say which timezone owns the schedule and what happens during DST gaps or repeated times.

I would avoid ambiguous strings and browser locale defaults in business logic. A well-tested date library or modern Temporal API can help, but I would still test timezone boundaries, DST transitions, and users far from the market timezone.

blocks.question: Why would a JavaScript application use dependency injection even without Angular?

blocks.question: A memoized selector returns stale data after an object is mutated. Why?

Memoization is only safe when the cache key really represents the inputs that affect the result. Many selectors cache by object identity. If the object is mutated in place, the reference stays the same, so the selector sees a cache hit and returns the old value.

That is why memoization and immutable state usually go together. When a meaningful value changes, the code should create a new object or update a version key. Then the cache can tell that the input changed.

I would also keep the cache bounded. A selector that accepts many argument combinations can quietly grow memory over the life of the app, especially in dashboards or long-lived tabs.

Before adding memoization, I would check that the function is pure and deterministic. If it depends on time, random values, external state, or mutation, caching makes bugs harder to see.

In production, I would measure hit rate and recompute cost. Memoization is useful when it removes repeated expensive work, not when it is added as a habit.

blocks.question: A framework uses Proxy to observe object changes. What benefits and risks should a senior developer understand?
blocks.answer:
A Proxy lets code intercept operations on an object, such as reading, writing, checking keys, deleting keys, or listing keys. Frameworks use that to build validation, lazy loading, reactive tracking, and virtual objects.

Reflect matters because it gives you the normal JavaScript operation in function form. Inside a proxy trap, calling Reflect.get or Reflect.set helps forward the operation with the right receiver and default behavior.

The risk is that proxies can make normal object rules feel magical. Identity checks may surprise people, serialization may not do what they expect, and private fields or built-in internal slots can fail when the receiver is wrong.

Performance is another concern. A proxy on a cold path is fine, but a proxy around every read in a hot rendering loop should be measured.

I would hide proxies behind a clear API. Application code should not need to know which objects are proxied or depend on trap side effects for basic correctness.

The first question is whether the browser should sort 500,000 records at all. For enterprise data, server-side sorting, indexed storage, pagination, or precomputed views are often better than making every client do heavy work.

If local sorting is required, I would remember that `Array.prototype.sort` mutates the array. Copying first may be correct for immutable state, but it doubles some memory pressure, so ownership matters.

The comparator must be consistent. It needs explicit rules for nulls, missing values, numeric strings, locale-aware text, and tie breakers. A flaky comparator can create unstable or confusing results.

For text sorting, `Intl.Collator` is usually better than hand-made locale rules, but I would create the collator once and reuse it. Creating it inside the comparator is a performance trap.

If the sort causes long tasks, I would move it to a Web Worker or sort only the data needed for the current view. Then I would profile on realistic devices, not just a fast laptop.

blocks.question: An application merges user-controlled JSON into a configuration object. What is prototype pollution and how do you prevent it?
blocks.answer:
Prototype pollution happens when user-controlled input changes an object's prototype chain instead of only setting normal data. In unsafe deep merges, keys like `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` can affect objects that were never meant to be touched.

The first defense is schema validation. I would accept only known configuration fields and reject unknown keys, especially dangerous keys at any nesting level.

I would also use maintained merge utilities that explicitly defend against this class of bug. For dictionary-like objects, `Object.create(null)` can help because there is no inherited prototype, but it is not a full substitute for validation.

Ownership checks matter when reading config. Code should use own-property checks and should not assume inherited properties are trusted data.

Security-sensitive defaults should stay server-controlled. A client-provided config should never be allowed to turn off authorization, logging, escaping, or other protections.

`eval` and `new Function` turn data into code. That creates injection risk, breaks strict content security policy, and makes code harder to analyze, cache, test, and debug.

For a rules engine, I would replace executable strings with a constrained rule format. A JSON expression tree or small declarative language can cover approved operations like comparisons, boolean logic, and field lookup.

The evaluator should parse and validate the rule before running it. It should limit nesting, operation count, and input size so a rule cannot become a denial-of-service problem.

The rule functions should not have access to globals, the DOM, cookies, storage, or network APIs. They should receive only the data needed for the rule.

If the product truly needs to run untrusted code, I would isolate it outside the main app context, such as a sandboxed separate origin. A normal app function is not a security boundary.

blocks.question: Where would you store preferences, cached data, drafts, and authentication material?

I would choose storage based on sensitivity, size, lifetime, and access pattern. There is no single browser storage API that is right for preferences, drafts, cached data, and authentication material.

For highly sensitive short-lived state, memory is safest because it disappears on refresh and is not directly persisted. For sessions, secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies are often better when the backend architecture supports them.

`localStorage` is only suitable for small, non-sensitive persistent values like UI preferences. It is synchronous and accessible to injected scripts, so it should not hold tokens or private data.

`sessionStorage` is useful for small per-tab state, but it is not a security boundary. It mainly helps separate tab lifetimes.

For large structured data, drafts, offline queues, and cached records, I would use IndexedDB with schema migration, cleanup, quota handling, and user or tenant partitioning.

The messages should be small, versioned, idempotent, and non-sensitive. A message can say 'logout happened' or 'tenant changed to X', but it should not carry secrets.

The server still owns authority. Cross-tab messaging improves UX, but session revocation and permission checks must be enforced by the backend.

blocks.question: A market-data WebSocket disconnects intermittently. Design a robust client.
blocks.answer:
A robust WebSocket client needs more than reconnecting in `onclose`. I would use bounded exponential backoff with jitter so many clients do not reconnect at the same time after an outage.

Retry behavior should respect app state. If the user is logged out, the browser is offline, or the tab is hidden for a long time, the client should stop or slow down instead of burning battery and backend capacity.

On connect, authentication should be safe and refreshable. I would avoid putting secrets in URLs or logs and make sure expired credentials do not create an endless reconnect loop.

For market data, sequence numbers matter. The client should track last message time, heartbeat, subscription state, and sequence gaps. After reconnect, it should resubscribe and request replay or a fresh snapshot if messages may have been missed.

The UI should show stale data clearly. Production monitoring should track reconnect count, lag, dropped messages, and gap recovery failures.

I would use content-hashed assets and a versioned cache manifest. From the service worker's point of view, the shell and the assets it needs should update as one compatible set.

The activation strategy needs a product decision. Some apps prompt users to refresh, some activate on next navigation, and some force reload only when losing in-progress work is not a risk.

API caching should not be one broad rule. Different endpoints need different freshness, user scoping, invalidation, and offline behavior.

There also needs to be a recovery path. If a cache is corrupted or a chunk is missing, the app should clear the right cache and reload without destroying drafts or local work.

blocks.question: Your application receives messages from an embedded iframe. How do you secure postMessage?

With `postMessage`, I treat every message as untrusted input. When sending sensitive messages, I would specify the exact target origin instead of using `*`.

On receipt, I would check `event.origin` against the expected origin and confirm `event.source` is the iframe or window I actually opened. Origin alone is not always enough when multiple frames are involved.

Then I would validate the message shape, version, and action. Only known actions should be accepted, and each action should validate its own payload.

Message data should never be evaled or inserted into HTML as trusted content. It is just input from another context.

For sensitive flows, I would use request IDs or nonces, keep secrets out of the iframe unless strictly needed, remove listeners on teardown, and log rejected messages without dumping private payloads.

blocks.question: Why can an ES module package still fail to tree-shake well?

Top-level side effects can keep a module alive. A file that registers globals, patches prototypes, injects CSS, or starts work at import time may not be safe to drop.

title: Coding: concurrency limiter
description: Senior/lead scenario: Run 1,000 asynchronous tasks but allow only five at a time. Design a concurrency limiter.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content: A concurrency limiter is a scheduler. It does not make tasks faster; it controls how many are allowed to run at once and preserves each task's completion semantics.
keyPoints: Maintain a queue and active count, start new work while active is below the limit, and start the next task in finally.
Return a promise for each submitted task and preserve its individual resolve/reject result.
Define whether one failure stops all work or only rejects that task.
Support cancellation, queue clearing, priority, and fairness only if required by the contract.
Test synchronous throws, fast resolution, rejection, and limit changes.

blocks.question: Run 1,000 asynchronous tasks but allow only five at a time. Design a concurrency limiter.
blocks.answer:
I would model the limiter with a queue and an active count. When a task is submitted, it waits until active work is below the limit, then starts.

Each submitted task should return its own promise. That promise resolves or rejects with that task's result, so callers do not lose individual failure information.

When a task finishes, the limiter should decrement the active count in a `finally` path and start the next queued task. This is important for both success and rejection.

The failure contract should be explicit. One rejected task may only reject that task, or it may stop the whole batch, depending on what the caller needs.

Extra features like cancellation, clearing the queue, priority, fairness, and dynamic limit changes are useful only if the contract requires them. I would test sync throws, immediate resolution, rejection, and never exceeding the limit.

title: Code review of nested callbacks
description: Senior/lead scenario: You find a callback-heavy function with duplicated error handling and hidden shared state. How would you refactor it?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content: Refactoring nested callbacks is about making control flow explicit. `async/await` improves readability only if the original dependencies, errors, and lifetimes are understood.
keyPoints: Identify the actual sequence and dependencies, then convert stable callback APIs to promises where appropriate.
Use small named functions for transformation and side effects, and keep one clear error boundary.
Pass required state explicitly rather than mutating outer variables from several branches.
Preserve cancellation and partial-success behavior; async/await syntax alone does not fix semantics.
Add characterization tests before refactoring high-risk production code.

blocks.question: You find a callback-heavy function with duplicated error handling and hidden shared state. How would you refactor it?
blocks.answer:
I would start by understanding the current behavior before changing syntax. Callback-heavy code often hides ordering, shared state, error handling, and partial-success rules.

If the callback APIs are stable and one-shot, I would wrap them in promises or use existing promise versions. Then `async` and `await` can make the sequence easier to read.

I would split transformation and side effects into small named functions. That makes each step testable and reduces the need for outer mutable variables.

Error handling should have one clear boundary where possible. Duplicated callback error branches often create inconsistent cleanup or different user behavior for similar failures.

Before refactoring risky production code, I would add characterization tests. The goal is to preserve cancellation, retry, partial success, and timing semantics, not just make the indentation prettier.

blocks.question: When is a callback still preferable to a promise?
blocks.answer: A callback is still preferable for repeated events, streaming data, or APIs where the producer calls the consumer many times over time. Promises represent one eventual result, so they are a poor fit for event listeners or long-running subscriptions. In those cases, callbacks, events, async iterators, or observables may match the contract better.

title: Security review of URL handling
description: Senior/lead scenario: The application redirects to a returnUrl query parameter after login. What checks are required?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content: Open redirects happen when navigation is treated as harmless. Redirect targets need the same kind of input validation as any other security-sensitive boundary.
keyPoints: Treat the value as untrusted and allow only internal paths or a strict allowlist of approved origins.
Parse with the URL API against a trusted base and reject dangerous schemes, protocol-relative URLs, encoded bypasses, and credential-bearing URLs.
Do not rely on startsWith for origin validation because look-alike hostnames and encoding can bypass naive checks.
Preserve only necessary parameters and avoid reflecting secrets into URLs or logs.
The server should enforce the same redirect policy where it participates in authentication.

blocks.question: The application redirects to a returnUrl query parameter after login. What checks are required?
blocks.answer:
A `returnUrl` is untrusted input. After login, I would allow only internal paths by default, or a strict allowlist of approved external origins if the product truly needs them.

I would parse the value with the `URL` API against a trusted base. That avoids many string parsing mistakes and lets the code inspect origin, protocol, pathname, username, and password fields clearly.

The code should reject dangerous schemes, protocol-relative URLs, encoded bypasses, look-alike hosts, and URLs with embedded credentials. `javascript:` and similar schemes should never be redirect targets.

I would not use `startsWith` for origin validation. Strings like `https://trusted.com.evil.com` or encoded variants can pass naive checks while pointing somewhere else.

Only necessary parameters should be preserved, and secrets should not be reflected into URLs or logs. If the server participates in auth redirects, it must enforce the same policy.

title: Senior JavaScript design judgment
description: Senior/lead scenario: A team wants to create a custom reactive framework, router, state store, and component library. As lead, how do you evaluate the proposal?

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content: Senior design judgment is about total cost and strategic fit. The question is not whether the team can build it; it is whether owning it is better than using and shaping the ecosystem around it.
keyPoints: Clarify the unsolved product problem and compare it with extending existing, maintained tools.
Estimate long-term ownership: browser changes, accessibility, security, testing, documentation, onboarding, and migration cost.
Prototype the narrow gap and measure the benefit. Avoid rebuilding infrastructure because the current API feels imperfect.
Adopt custom infrastructure only where it creates strategic differentiation or satisfies constraints existing tools cannot meet.
If approved, define a minimal scope, public contract, maintenance team, and exit strategy.

blocks.question: A team wants to create a custom reactive framework, router, state store, and component library. As lead, how do you evaluate the proposal?
blocks.answer:
I would start by asking what product problem is not solved by existing tools. Building a framework, router, state store, and component library is a long-term ownership decision, not just an engineering preference.

Then I would compare the proposal with extending maintained tools. Sometimes the right answer is a thin abstraction, a plugin, or a design-system layer instead of a full custom platform.

The team needs to account for browser changes, accessibility, security, testing, documentation, onboarding, migrations, and support. Those costs continue long after the fun prototype works.

If there is a real gap, I would prototype the narrowest part of it and measure the benefit. A custom system should exist because it creates strategic value or satisfies constraints existing tools cannot meet.

If approved, I would define a minimal public contract, owners, maintenance process, compatibility policy, and exit strategy. Custom infrastructure without ownership becomes a product risk.
